text:
There are a lot of great things being said here, but I don't like the implication that anxiety disorders are somehow not real. No one is saying that anxiety itself is a disorder... Obviously it's an emotion, but it becomes a disorder when it interferes with your ability to function in everyday life. Sadness is an emotion too, but if you're experiencing it to such a high degree that you take your own life, it's clearly not normal. Happiness is an emotion, but if it's so intense that you're manic, it's not healthy. Going to the bathroom is normal, but if you're going 30 times a day something is probably wrong.

Anxiety doesn't make me anxious because I think I'm sick or some bs, it makes me anxious because I know it's going to affect my ability to function. If anything, it's validating knowing it's my brain's fault, not my own, and it's not just that I'm weak willed or have a moral failing. Our brains are part of our bodies, mental health isn't somehow not medical just because we don't fully understand it.

text:
I remember…back in high school…I once wrote an essay about toxic positivity. I wrote it because it was the only way I felt I could communicate my feelings in a safe way. To get someone to notice without condemnation, scorn, or bewilderment. I had carried a looming, unbearable feeling of hopelessness for years, despite having straight A’s, and living the life of a model student. I was constantly told that I was special, loved, and blessed. That I had nothing to be sad about…but those words of comfort were sharper and more damaging than any insult or hateful actions that could have been used against me. As a kid, I was never bullied. I was never abused, never suffered any financial struggles, or lacked basic necessities…but what I needed more than any of that was what I was starved of: emotional attention. I couldn’t be sad because I had to be perfect inside and out. I had to be grateful for what I had, and being depressed was always seen as taking things for granted. I didn’t deserve to be distressed.
 So I had to smile. I had to try and contain the hurricane within myself with a bottle. A bottle which I couldn’t keep shut. And the longer I tried to ignore it, the more it threatened to shatter. But I couldn’t let it out because no one gave me room for tears. No room for anger. No room for negativity. Because, as far as they were concerned, my life was too perfect to justify the thoughts of self-loathing, hopelessness, and worthlessness I battled with every day. Warring with the hurricane when all I had to fight it with was a bottle and the smile people forced upon me as a pathetic excuse for an umbrella. So I turned to writing my feelings out on paper, and I wrote that essay with the intention of shedding some light on toxic positivity, so that maybe even one less person would have to suffer through the same silent torment I did. We need to be more compassionate, understanding, and less condemning of others’ fears and feelings just because of their physical circumstances. Because material wealth is replaceable, whereas a person’s life is not. We as humans are far more complex than our physical blessings, so stop treating us as such. To everyone out there, reach out to those you feel are hurting or hiding something. Because they may just be waiting for that one person to show that they care.

text: The physiological sigh that Huberman talks about is something I use constantly in my facilitation work. Two short inhales through the nose followed by an extended exhale through the mouth. It works because the double inhale pops open the alveoli in your lungs that have collapsed, maximizing surface area for gas exchange. The long exhale then activates the parasympathetic nervous system through the vagus nerve. What I find in practice is that combining this with cold exposure creates a much deeper training effect. When someone is sitting in 3 degree water and their body is in full sympathetic activation, using breath control to deliberately shift into calm is the most powerful stress inoculation I have seen. The skill transfers directly to high pressure situations outside the water. After six years of running these sessions I still find it remarkable how fast people can shift their state once they understand the mechanism.

text:
Okay for those of you who found this helpful, I'm happy for you. That's awesome. But as I see it, this can be INCREDIBLY harmful advice. There is a difference between "anxiety" the emotion and "anxiety" the disorder. Just as there's a difference between "depression" the emotion and "depression" the disorder. Yeah, everyone feels anxious sometimes, everyone feels depressed at some point in their lives. But it becomes a disorder when it literally changes your brain chemistry and affects your daily functioning. Mental illness is real. And it's not just a label that doctors came up with to make us feel bad.

One thing that is flat-out wrong in this talk is the claim that anxiety is purely a mental condition and not medical. Mental illness is absolutely a medical problem. Your anxiety affects your physical health and vice versa. And it's not something that you can just think your way out of. Your brain isn't trying to make you happy. It's trying to keep you alive. And for some people, anxiety really isn't there for any good reason or the level of anxiety is so drastically disproportionate to the cause that it makes daily life feel impossible. Dismissing a legit medical condition as a completely normal, run-of-the-mill, friendly emotion and saying it's "easy" to just get over it is SO dangerous for so many reasons.

It's invalidating. When you try to just shift your perception of anxiety and be happy about it but then the simplest, stupidest little thing makes you want to burst into tears or explode, it's absolutely horrible. I hate myself in these times because I "should" be fine and this "should" be easy and it's "not a big deal." But I still feel awful, so what's wrong with me? That's the kind of thing this toxic positivity attitude does to me. There comes a point where it's NOT normal and your brain consistently overcompensates and goes way too far trying to protect you from threats. Saying "Everyone gets anxious" to someone with an anxiety disorder is like saying "Everyone gets kinda sad sometimes" to someone with major depressive disorder or saying "Everyone has trouble focusing sometimes" to someone with ADHD or saying "Everyone struggles to understand social cues sometimes" to someone with autism. These aren't things that can just be fixed by changing your perspective.

ALSO this kind of attitude can make people even less likely to get treatment. Being diagnosed with anything doesn't mean "Yep you're broken and there's nothing you can do about it." People don't go through several years of intense schooling just to say that to patients. Having a name for a condition means you're not alone and you're not broken and there's a reason you're struggling. And it means there is SO much you can do about it. Therapy can be extremely helpful and medication can be extremely helpful. There are several widespread anxiety medications that aren't addictive controlled substances, and even the controlled substances can be life-changing. There's a reason people get medication. It can help you to actually function in the world. There's a reason people dedicate their entire lives and careers into the research and treatment of mental health conditions. It's making a big difference in the world.

You say it's important to stop being scared of anxiety. But I say it's important to stop being scared of anxiety diagnosis and treatment. Ignoring the problem won't make it go away. You can absolutely be loving and understanding and kind to yourself about your anxiety. You can learn to accept it so you can do something about it. Validating yourself in that it makes sense why you're feeling the way that you do is important. But that doesn't mean it's not a problem. Identifying problems leads to solutions.

So please just recognize that not all advice will work for everybody. Present your opinions just as opinions and not facts. And while the views and experience of someone who has a condition can be very valuable, I just think you should be extremely careful talking so confidently about medical treatment if you aren't qualified as a medical professional. Especially actively discouraging diagnosis and sometimes life-saving treatment.

So I'm sorry if I'm being a wet blanket or annoying or something, but this message really rubbed me the wrong way. And I think (and hope) I'm not alone in that. Do whatever helps you, and have a good day.

text: This video topic makes me think, so much, about the following quote from 2011 Restoration Therapy Understanding and Guiding Healing in Marriage Family Therapy. In the book, the author, Dr. Terry Hargrave, writes the following Another way that people who protect themselves from perceived lack of safety in relationships through control behaviors is to be performance driven. Typical of this type of performancedriven behavior is the wish by someone to absolutely ensure that that there is no perceived vulnerability in terms of safety. If, for example, the controller determines that he or she could be safe by having a financial savings account of 10,000, he or she would likely work to achieve the goal. But, after the goal was achieved, he or she would discover that the financial vulnerability still existed in other words, the person might have saved 10,000, but they still FEEL unsafeinsecurefinancially vulnerable. He or she would feel driven perhaps to double the amount of money to 20,000. Of course, no matter how much money the controller saved, he or she would still feel vulnerable and then have expectations about how he or she should handle or invest the money. In other words, each step of performance with the money sets the stage for a more complicated and higher performance level. Controllers often find this performance double bind with finances, achievement, education, status, and career, just to name a few areas of struggle. At each new rung of performance achievement, the controller finds that there is no more a sense of safety than at the previous rung. But, instead of going back or assuming that the pursuit of performance is futile, the controller will often press on to a higher performance level, hoping that the next rung will provide the sense of security, safety, and lack of anxiety that is sought. To me, this video of yours, Dr. K., is all about performancedriven individuals. These individuals often have a terrible sense of self identity, and sometimes will cope with it by simply being down and depressed. But many of these individuals learn a reactive mechanism in life, which is that When I perform well, other people like that, and they acknowledgepraisenotice me. That is certainly better than feeling bad about myself. What if I just become the person who performs really well with everything I do? Wouldn't that guarantee that people like me, since I would always be performing well? I then watch these individuals go on to burn themselves out with the neverending performative lifestyle. I wish for these people to heal and do better for themselves. It really is painful when you get caught in the trap of trying to perform your way out of your bad sense of identity into a good one. And it sucks even more when you realize that your performances in life have not built a new, better identity but instead have amounted to no more than a false, pseudoidentity that really is not who you are deep down. I had a "quack" tell me years ago that suicidal thoughts are normal - it is only a question of whether you've ever acted on them.  At the time I thought he was dismissive, overworked and didn't take me seriously - well - come to find out - that quack knew his stuff....and that was 30 years ago.  I still have thoughts of suicide most days of my life.  I think it has become a crutch.  IF things get too bad - I will just end it...and then I feel a sense of relief and I can go on about my day.  The thought of ending it all somehow brings me relief - it's crazy, I know, but it acts like an emotional escape hatch.  I am certainly not being glib about it - it's a painful process and eats away at my soul a little each time.

Til this day - I have never acted on it but I do try to imagine how I would do it.  For 30 years I have always found a reason not to - and it's usually put on someone else's shoulders.  Today, my excuse is to not leave my husband of 72 alone to deal with our house, our bills, etc.  I just couldn't do that to him.  

I am 59 years old, I am terrified over my own mortality.  I think life has been equal parts cruel and joyous.  I love life but hate MY life and think about my failures incessantly.  My obsessive thoughts take me to dark places most days - so, I work, do my daily mundane chores to keep my mind from "going there".  I (barely) sleep but when i do its always with my computer and the tv on.  Quiet spaces are brutal.  So, I sleep four hours a day, run myself ragged....lather - rinse - repeat. What else can you do.

Your "talk" was insightful, and it is about time that people like you start looking outside the box.  This 100-year cookie cutter approach needs a tune up.  I have been saying this for years about the 12-step program for alcohol/addiction.  IT DOESN'T WORK for most people - statistics tell us that every day.  I hope this leads to new and innovative ways of recognizing this and with treatment that actually helps.

text: Does everything need to be framed from a deficit orientated perspective? I don't know what branch of therapy you do if its CBT or which theories you follow and base your opinion on. But I see it as a great resources if someone is able to overcome challenges and transform them into something positive. Wouldn't you say that that's a resource? Only viewing the possible negatives about a behavior doesn't paint the full picture. Resource orientation is crucial for the client. While understanding whats wrong can help the client gain insight, it doesnt necessarily empower them to make change. In fact, it can even weaken their sense of Self efficacy. Supporting clients to identify and build on their existing strengths helps them create more functional routines and sustainable change. So, while I understand your point about always pushing through and not making changes when it's necessary, I think that message doesnt have to come across in such a deficit orientated way. This also raises an important question. Is the deficit focused framing used to encourage people to seek coaching or paid support? If that's true, isnt that ethically problematic? text:
Whilst I understood that a nervous breakdown isn't a term used now, I always assumed it was a term used years ago by doctors. My mother had what she always described as a nervous breakdown 40 years ago and I'm sure she said this is what the doctors told her that she had experienced. Although something could have been lost in translation here. 

My mother wandered out of a supermarket without paying for her shopping, but when confronted, the staff realised something was seriously wrong with her. Luckily they called the authorities who admitted her to hospital and took my sister and I into care. My mother was experiencing catatonic depression, suffered with dry eyes (because she hardly blinked) and an inability to feel pain. She said that it would take ages for her to light a cigarette but then she would just let it burn down to her fingers and she wouldn't even feel it. She had to re learn even simple things like making a cup of tea (which left her exhausted afterwards) and spent two years in a psychiatric ward. 

I know that she experienced severe panic attacks at some point in those two years also but that's about the extent of my knowledge. Unfortunately she still wasn't very well when she was released and I was returned to her. She never seemed to fully recover mentally and had severe depressive episodes for the rest of her life. Apparently, she was a fun loving, bright and enthusiastic person until her 'breakdown.' I wonder how differently things may have turned out if she was treated nowadays. 

Although the saddest part is that she was left on her own with two children and no support, meaning no one noticed how ill she had become to begin with. She weighed 6 stone when she wandered out of the supermarket as she had stopped eating, so there were physical signs too. It speaks to how we really do need to take care of each other as a community and how damaging isolation can really be.

Beautyfully spoken about trauma but when she will begin talking about occupational burnout:

Burn-out is included in the 11th Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) as an occupational phenomenon. It is not classified as a medical condition.

It is described in the chapter: ‘Factors influencing health status or contact with health services’ – which includes reasons for which people contact health services but that are not classed as illnesses or health conditions.

Burn-out is defined in ICD-11 as follows:

“Burn-out is a syndrome conceptualized as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It is characterized by three dimensions:

feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion;
increased mental distance from one’s job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism related to one's job; and
reduced professional efficacy.
Burn-out refers specifically to phenomena in the occupational context and should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life.”

Burn-out was also included in ICD-10, in the same category as in ICD-11, but the definition is now more detailed.

The World Health Organization is about to embark on the development of evidence-based guidelines on mental well-being in the workplace.

text: A few lifehacks from a senior dev, 10y exp, having burnt out twice in my career before. Slack off from day 1, do the bare minimum at the longest pace you can. They're definitely going to fire me isn't a thing until you've had a 11 talk or a few with your direct manager about your poor performance. Until then, they're fine with your pace. Find a company that's going to be fine with your slacker pace. This is important, because you can have more personal time while also finishing your job on time as is fine with them. Crunching also becomes more rewarding and easier to plan, e.g. you can have an entire day off after the daily calls and then crunch 23 tasks the next day. This changes everything and reduces the stress drastically. Violate schedules, don't show up to useless meetings. This one is also about pushing the limits of slacking. Make it the norm for them to accept you not coming to a meeting provided it actually is pointless to you. You can say things like I don't have any more questions regarding this topic, so I'll skip the meeting or I'll watch the recording at another time to absorb the information, etc. You can use work as an excuse too, I really want to focus on this task instead, etc. If you manage to do it, this will alleviate a lot of stress. Actually read the handbook to see how much time you have to respond to chat messages and emails. Usually chat messages are limited to 46h within the work hours and emails are limited to 1 business day. Use it to your advantage. Listen to your feelings when hearing the messageemail notification and ask yourself, am I stable enough mentally right now to take a look at this message? If not, leave it for much later. If it's in the handbook, you're allowed to do this. Aint no way there's a company that will allow me to do all of this you'd be surprised. It may take a year or more of job hopping to actually find a company like this, but they do exist. Consider a lower paycheck too, because it's the money worth sacrificing for your own well being. And if you have a spouse, a kid, etc, then it's the money that will be sacrificed for their sake too. Currently you can't pay 10ky to be able to spend 15h a week more with your family, but you can make it a reality.

text:
Think of anxiety as a more unpredictable and longer lasting type of fear. Fear is future based and relief of forethought to be brought into being. You can easily prove this to yourself by trying to fear something that has happened in the past... something that really scared you and had you fearing in the moment it happened - try it. Try to put yourself in the same fearful state again. You can't. So just know that fear is future based. Picture it like this - when something of high importance is about to happen to you, and the outcome of it is uncertain, your awareness projects itself into a future where the worst likely scenario has happened. The mind takes that feeling of the worst outcome, and then goes back to the present and manifests that feeling in you. That's the process of fear. Knowing this will already put you miles ahead of anyone else :)
Now, to easiest thing you can do to eliminate the fear is to not let your awareness go into the future to paint that FALSE picture. That is, do this only if you're certain that the thing you're fearing is just your minds made up BS, like stressing over a presentation or important confrontation. Tell yourself "I'm alright right now." - this keeps you in the now and brings you back to reality.
Hope this helps yall :)

text: The biggest problem I've seen is the constant disconnect between budgetexpectations and the work itself. People at the top or product managers, for example, often do not even understand the scope of work on a macro level. An easy way to spot this is when determining the age old question of, How long will this take? The devs say 23 weeks. The manager says, Ok, let's do it in 4 days and we need a POC by Friday morning. This arbitrary goalpost then forces the devs to work overtime, usually without pay, and in overdrive mode, to try and meet this deadline. The code quality is worse, the bugs are everywhere, but we can move fast and break things. If things fail, who gets blamed, do you think? Good code is almost never the goal because it isn't realistically attainable with these undervalued restraints. This toxic viewpoint is in almost every dev environment I've ever been in, even in the good companies I've worked for. It's a lack of respect for the work and the actual ability of these very talented people and I wish it would stop, but there is no incentive for it to. Too many people, much similar to artists, are eager to prove themselves and even for free if need be do I even bother bringing up the entire slave internship dilemma?. Then you have open source. A beautiful construct of community work and innovation, which is, of course, exploited once again and further contributes to this perception. Entire swathes of companies and corporations are built on someone else's free software. I love what I do and the challenge, and honestly most devs I know got in it for the same reasons. This passion is often what gives us an unnatural resilience, but it also creates a serious mountain that is impossible for most thus the burnout. Luckily, I made it on top of my mountain, but I cannot fathom being a junior or even just starting out in this climate, especially with the ascent of AI. The next generation will only get it even worse unless something significant changes. The market will not fix this problem because it does not want the best product, it wants the cheapest. text: To everyone who's studying with this music: Checklist: • A bottle of water, at least 1liter. Your brain works better if it has enough water and drinking helps you to concentrate • Your charger. text: It's funny. I burned out on exercise and training, figured out I was pushing myself too hard. I got an education in IT and became a dev. At the interview I was told that I would work with legacy and renewing it. I knew this was a very unpopular type of work, but I just wanted to get into the field. Idk what happened mentally, but the second I secured the job, I immediately checked out of responsibility. I worked far less than I'm required to do, but my company is actually pretty cool with it. And I accepted the fact that I would suck for several years. This last one is important, because many feel a lot of pressure to be really awesome when they are a beginner. When you're new to something, anything, you will suck regardless. So just embrace it. I'm going to be trash at this for the next 5 years, but in 23 years I'll be ok. Here's what I learned from my training. I was doing Japanese martial arts, which I think is important. A part of the traditional training is to push you past a breaking point. And then you do it again and again. Although it will fuck you up, the idea is to develop a mindset where you can get past adversity with flying colors. And ironically, when pushed to the edge a hundred times over, you learn that you have to be smart. You can't push your body and mind past the breaking point without breaking. If we look to the ancient writings of the most legendary sword masters, they don't talk about technique. It's all about the mind. And when I read Japanese history, the strategy during war was to always fight the easiest battle. Because winning was the goal. So I have an old document that says that you should never battle a spear master with a spear. You shoot him with a bow. In other words, never fight on the enemy's terms. You set your own terms. Taking this back to the modern world, your goals are most likely at odds with your employer. Their ultimate goal is highly experienced employees who work 247 with no pay. Your ultimate goal is probably to just do whatever the fuck you want and have some means of supporting that life. As long as you provide just enough for them to value your labor over looking for someone else, you should do the absolute minimum unless you enjoy it and want to do more. Focus on whatever are your personal goals and do what it takes. Don't be spellbound by the bullshit. text:
I think, I understand the reason for my panic attacks. It is normal fear that I don’t want to admit to myself. 
All my life I had a feeling, that I just had to push through with some things without caring about my feelings. 

For example, I was shy and got bad grades for not participating in class. My teachers and my parents just said: You just have to stop being shy, it will get you nowhere. Just say something during class. 
(I’m from Germany, maybe the teachers are especially insensitive here.)
Nobody asked me why I felt shy and no one tried to comfort me. 

There were multiple situations in my life where my feelings weren’t considered and where I was just told to push through. 

I often had panic attacks while driving, which started after my partner and I went on vacation to Denkmark. My partner didn’t have a drivers license then and I just said: „I‘ll drive us to Denmark for six hours.“ and I drove us right after a stressful workday. I couldn’t admit to myself that it was stressful and that I was overwhelmed. 
So the panic attacks started. 

Now that I can more easily admit it to myself when things overwhelm me, panic attacks are going away. 

I try to be honest and communicate when I need help.

text: I've been a software developer for over 10 years and worked at several companies. A lot of the points brought up here I have never experienced. Maybe it's a US vs. UK approach to work or just where I've worked but I doubt it. The point about working super late and on weekends isn't something I've seen. Most mature companies and managers know that the valuable employees, those who have been there a long time and accrued knowledge, can easily get a job elsewhere so burning them out is a bad long term plan. Most people I've worked with technical and non technical know that problems arise and that things can slip past the estimates, it's not a blame game and people know that software developers are doing their best. I've also not seen the narcissistic boss thing either, they know that if software developers say something isn't feasible within a certain amount of time, pushing people harder doesn't make features appear out of thin air. Here's what I think the real cause is there's no time for general maintenance. Most other engineering disciplines have standards and safety procedures that are set, offices are usually cleaned regularly and other routine tasks are handled by other people. In software development, the demands are featurefeaturefeaturebugfixmeetingsfeatures and no alloted time for maintenance. On the outside it's new features but under the hood we're building on top of things that need to be cleaned up, dumping more code in is so horrible. Imagine a kitchen where cooks pump out meals but it's never cleaned, would you look forward to going back to work the next day? Probably not. You have to either clean up without anyone noticing or really pushing for more time to do it. Software development is misunderstood by a lot of people, it is both technical and creative. We start with learning the basics and having a good technical foundation, eventually moving on to using the knowledge to build something with whatever approach you choose. The combination of both of those is very satisfying but it demands long periods of uninterrupted time an hour at least and there's always someone who wants an answer to a mundane question right away. That is one of the things that really bothers me the most, it may be different for others.

text:
Gotta give this video a like. I don't suffer with anxiety like some people in the comments do. But I loved the talk, and I do hope it helps. It sounds like it does from the comments.

Even though I don't suffer from anxiety, I have certainly felt anxiety during my life. One of the things I've noticed about anxiety is that it's often fear over a possible outcome, which might never happen.

In other words, it's not some made up fear. It's a real possibility, even if it's not the only possible outcome. Over the years, I've evaluated these fears, and I'm often surprised after the event that caused the anxiety is over. I'm surprised because, while the fears were based on real possibilities, they omitted possible positive outcomes, and the result was usually far better than the fears wanted me to believe.

I have changed employment for what I hoped would be a better career from careers that were already decent, moved between states, bought homes, and I served in combat zones in three countries.

In all these cases, anxiety wanted to hold me back. "You don't need this!" "Things could get worse if you do this!" "What if you fail?" "What if someone is better than you?" Or even, "You could die." These and many other thoughts ate at me.

I started to do the following...which seems to be inline with this talk. I would ask myself, "What am I anxious about?" I would try to answer this honestly and completely. I would then say, "What's the worst thing that could happen?"...the crux of the fear. Once I determined this, I would then ask myself, "Is there anything I can do to make this bad outcome less likely if I decide to take this path?" Planning and preparing seem to reduce anxiety...at least for me. I would finally say, "What good could come of this? And, how valuable would it be in my life?"

Because of these questions, I have been a computer programmer, a logistics specialist, a soldier, and a project manager. And more importantly a father and husband. 

Probably very few if any people will read this comment, but if you are one of the few, I hope it helps.

Anxiety may be an emotion that's trying to help us avoid danger or negative outcomes, it just shouldn't get 100% of the decision making power in our lives.

text: I will say that sometimes actually many times this can be avoided. Today's world seems to be an abyss as I told my subscribers in this week's topic. People have a sense of feeling lost. Many are in the emotional depths so deep they feel they are about to be overwhelmed internally--aka the breakdown. I've been close to this twice in my life. Once at 22 for social reasons as I had no social ability with others especially the opposite sex. I was also at the bottom ranks of the enlisted military with no trade to my name. And once at 31 as I graduated college with a physical therapy degree, flunked the boards in a field that just went south with no jobs thanks to severe medicare cuts. I solved both with this simple task. It really is this simple. You take a piece of paper and on one side write the problem. On the other side the solution. In the middle you write the strategy to get there. Then at the bottom of the page you write each strategy and subdivide what you have to do to make that strategy happen. IE. Problem: no PT license. Solution: become a licensed therapist. In the middle : Strategy: pass the board test. Subdivide. 1 ) take a class for the exam 2) study for it for four months. This simple method visually puts in your mind--yes, this is what I need to do and here is what I do to get there. By being proactive the mind veers away from the breakdown point instead of spinning its wheels in panic which over time is what leads to the breakdown. And you can use this method for anything plaguing your life to climb out of the abyss. Hope this helps someone out there---Charles

text: The Neuropsychology of relaxation and a novel procedure for sustaining relaxation that it entails Much ink has been spilled on describing the neuropsychology of stress, but very little on the neuropsychology of relaxation, which is surprisingly simple, yet has been overshadowed by its incorrect appellation as a meditative state. Here is an explanation and novel procedure for sustaining relaxation that ironically has little to do with meditation. In a 1984 article in the flagship journal of the APA, The American Psychologist, the psychologist David Holmes reviewed the literature on meditation and concluded that meditative states are no different from resting states. The article linked below was roundly criticized because resting was presumably a dormant and nonaffective state, quite at odds with the fact that meditation has affective and cognitive entailments that go beyond mere resting. However, from the perspective of affective neuroscience, resting states are not simple nonaffective states but are dynamic affective states that are continually modulated by information derived from inner thoughts to outward perceptions. This position is not difficult to understand, and can be summarized below and easily falsified through simple procedure. The ideal for any scientist with a great idea is to be able to explain it in a minute, and to confirm or falsify it as quickly. The world record for this arguably goes to the English philosopher Samuel Johnson, who rejected Archbishop Berkeleys argument that material things only exist in ones mind by striking his foot against a large stone while proclaiming, I refute it thusly! So here is a novel procedure demonstrating the continuity of rest from mindful to flow states, quickly refutable with a good swift kick! Summary Endogenous opioids are induced when we eat, drink, have sex, and relax, and are responsible for our pleasures. Opioid activity however is not static, but labile, or changeable. When elicited, opioid release is always modulated by concurrently perceived novel actoutcome expectancies which may range from negative to positive. If they are negative e.g. a spate of bad news or bad implications of our behavior, opioid activity is suppressed and our pleasures are reduced anhedonia, but if they are positive, then opioid activity is enhanced and our pleasures are accentuated as well peak experience, flow. This is due to dopamineopioid interactions, or the fact that actoutcome discrepancy, or positive or negative surprises, can induce or suppress dopaminergic activity, which in turn can enhance or suppress opioid release. This can be demonstrated procedurally, and if correct, can provide a therapeutic tool to increase arousal and pleasure, or positive wellbeing, and mitigate stress. Basic Facts Endogenous opioids are induced when we eat, drink, have sex, and relax. Their affective correlate, or how it feels, is a sense of pleasure. The neuromodulator dopamine is released upon the anticipation or perception of positive actoutcome discrepancy or novelty, and is felt a sense of arousal or energy, but not pleasure. Fun Fact When we are concurrently perceiving some activity that has a variable and unexpected rate of reward while consuming something pleasurable, opioid activity increases and with it a higher sense of pleasure. In other words, popcorn tastes better when we are watching an exciting movie than when we are watching paint dry. The same effect occurs when we are performing highly variable rewarding or meaningful activity creating art, doing good deeds, doing productive work while in a pleasurable relaxed state. Meaning would be defined as behavior that has branching novel positive implications. This is commonly referred to as flow or peak experience. The same phenomenon underscores the placebo effect, which describes how expectancies can increase dopamine and opioid activity, such as when a meal is tastier or a sugar pill reduces pain when we anticipate they will. So why does this occur? DopamineOpioid interactions or the fact that dopamine activity elicited by positive novel events, and responsible for a state of arousal, but not pleasure interacts with our pleasures as reflected by mid brain opioid systems, and can actually stimulate opioid release, which is reflected in selfreports of greater pleasure. Proof or kicking the stone Just get relaxed using a relaxation protocol such as progressive muscle relaxation, eyes closed rest, or mindfulness, and then follow it by exclusively attending to or performing meaningful activity, and avoiding all meaningless activity or distraction. Keep it up and you will not only stay relaxed, but continue so with a greater sense of wellbeing or pleasure. In other words, this is a procedural bridge between mindful and flow experiences that are not unique psychological states, but merely represent special aspects of resting states. The attribution of affective value to meaningful behavior makes the latter seem autotelic, or reinforcing in itself, and the resultant persistent m to meaning o out the occasions we might have spent dwelling on other meaningless worries and concerns. A Likely Explanation, as if you need one! A more formal explanation from a neurologically based learning theory of this technique is provided on pp. 4451 in a little opensource book on the psychology of rest linked below. The flow experience discussed on pp. 8186. The book is based on the work of the distinguished affective neuroscientist Kent Berridge, who was kind to review for accuracy and endorse the work. From meditation to flow Affect in rest is labile, or changeable, and rest i.e. the general deactivation of the covert musculature is not an inert and nonaffective state, but modulates affective systems in the brain. In addition, the degree of the modulation of pleasurable affect induced by rest is not dependent upon a species of attention focal meditation, mindfulness meditation, but is schedule dependent, and correlates with the variability of schedules or contingencies of reward and the discriminative aspects of incentives i.e. their cognitive implications. In other words, sustained meaningful activity or the anticipation of acting meaningfully during resting states increases the affective tone or value of that behavior, thus making productive work autotelic, or rewarding in itself, and providing a consistent feeling of arousal and pleasure, or shall we say, happiness. Better stop the music or put on different music for the break. Open your window, even if it's cold outside. Fresh air will make it better, trust me. I think the answer is measuring what you can sustainably do in the long run to achieve your goal. What doctor K. said at the end was really helpful, you have to find that baseline happiness or something like worklife balance, or in this case, effort and mental balance. Practice and working hard usually suck. If you have really ambitious goals having to work hard is probably not something that can be avoided. But by accepting the you of right now the stress and pressure of performance might go down, which makes that sort of concentrated effort easier. If you don't have your ego riding on whether you're a grindset kinda guy then you'll 1 have less stress around the task 2 will be able to avoid longterm burnout and constant quitting because you'll be able to recognize your limits better or when you might need a break, instead of pushing through. By deattaching from the highs and lows and just learning to take it day by day and not putting such high emotional stakes you can keep on practicing for a longer span of time. The ego also causes us to make up deadlines I want to be better than this person in x amount of time, or 'my music should sound like y soon or I've failed'. What we're trying to do is make the goods and bads matter less. You might also not like what you find out, maybe you can only handle 3 hours of making music a week before you feel miserable. Then you either have to find a way to be less miserable what that looks like could be different, maybe it's making music with friends, or maybe you reward yourself with something, or try and poke at what's causing the misery and try and lessen it etc or you'll have to accept that that's the pace you'll be going at, and it might take you a while longer, but you'll still be doing what you care for and improving.

text: While I appreciate this clear distinction between burnout and depression, I find the solutions presented here a bit more individualcentered than Dr. Maslach's most recent work. In The Burnout Challenge, she emphasizes 'rethinking burnout' by shifting the weight onto the systemic environment rather than the individual. She famously uses the 'canary in the coal mine' allegory if a canary dies in a toxic mine, we don't try to make the canary more resilient or teach it 'yoga'we fix the mine. While personal coping mechanisms like boundaries and sleep are vital for mental health, focusing solely on 'learning ways to cope' can inadvertently turn wellness into a bandaid. It risks shifting the burden of a systemic issue onto the individual, allowing organizations to avoid addressing the core 'mismatches'like workload or lack of fairnessthat cause the burnout in the first place. Id love to see more discussion on how we can move from individual resilience to organizational accountability!

I have been a loner, disconnected from people since I was young, always kept to myself, never socially gifted, maybe jealous of other people who seemed able to get along with everyone, always have a smile on their face, never have a care in the world.  I feel that no one wants to be troubled by my problems so I don't talk about it.  This keeps me from maintaining relationships. Do I actually want to die or do I just not want to feel this way anymore, it's probably more not wanting to feel and thinking maybe being dead means I won't feel this way.  But how do we ever know?  Those who have ended themselves and their lives with the rest of us won't come back and tell me if it's better for them to be dead than alive.  
I ask myself, if I am dead, will it matter to anyone?  Or if I end my life, how will it effect people who I think might care about me?  That is the Catch-22, damned if I do, damned if I don't situation that tortures me.  Some days I feel more okay, but there is always lingering doubt in the deep crevices that maybe I AM worthless, that I'm not worthwhile.
Guess the above is why I have made music under the moniker "Tommy Psychosis".  Both a nom de plume and a type of mental illness.

not that i wanted to make this public either, but had a similarly stressful situation(no pass out thankfully, but i dropped my purse).  Planned Parenthood: general pap smear, urine test done beforehand.  The moment I leave the bathroom after passing the specimen through the little slot inside the restroom, a nurse is waiting right outside the door.  She is beaming and happily says, "You're pregnant Mommy!"  This is when my purse fell to the ground&I started feeling faint.  I was in my mid-thirties, bf was told by a doc@age 18 it would be unlikely he would be able to get anyone pregnant due to low sperm count, but he had made it clear he did not want children.  In the waiting room b4 giving the sample, I had to fill out a questionnaire about what my wishes were for the baby if I was pregnant.  I filled in the radio button that said I wanted to keep it.  He was looking over my shoulder and said, "Are you sure?"
All kinds of thoughts were racing through my head:  "How could they possibly check my sample so quickly?  Am I going to end up a single Mother working two jobs just like my own Mother did when I was a latch-key kid?  How am I going to be able to afford this situation I was never expecting on my $7/hr grocery store cashier wage?  I don't have health insurance.  How do I tell my bf?  Do I tell my bf?  What is my Mother going to think since she hates my bf?
I am sat down inside a back room with the door closed about to call my Mother w/the good news when the door opens.  Prior to this, they would not stop calling me "Mommy" while taking my blood pressure as I was having a panic attack. Nurse Ratchet told me to calm down and "think about the baby."  The door opens, it's a different nurse.  She apologizes and tells me the urine samples got mixed up and I actually am not pregnant.  The call to my Mother was just seconds away from going through.  I hang up on her.  A wave of relief mixed with regret and remorse washes over me.  "This means your $75 pap smear is going to be FREE on the house today!"  I feel ambivalent in response.  I wonder if this person is going to make a mistake during the pelvic examination and have anxiety about being a patient in this facility...but it's been years since I've had an exam, and I'm already here...and my bf is at the library waiting for me to call when I'm done.  At least all I have to do is lie on a table.  I clutch the welcome baby pack I was given for would-be mothers and get the exam.  It goes swimmingly, thankfully.  All Clear.  As I leave the facility, the nurse who told me I was preggers tells me, "You don't have to tell your bf about this."  Are you KIDDING ME???! I'm telling everyone: my co-workers, my family, anyone who will listen.
Then she notices the piece of paper I have in my hand that reads: Confirmation of Pregnancy.  "We need that PAPER!."  Without thinking I hand it to her and she IMMEDIATELY SHREDS IT!  Then she eyes the welcome package for new mothers that contains an actual diaper.  She wants this as well!  I tell her I want to keep it and she lets me.  I still feel like there may be a possibility I'm pregnant and wonder about getting a second opinion and was it a mistake to get the pap smear?  For the next week, and months later...I am a basket case.

text: So what's being said here is... Feeling overwhelmed is actually the feeling of losing control. When shit rains down and it feels too much. So break the anxiety by doing something you do have control over. Or do something you are capable of doing with the resources you have right now. Even if it's completely unrelated to the problems that overwhelm you, it will bring back the feeling of being able make a difference in your life. For me that's cleaning my home. When my space is in order I magically start to feel like I can tackle anything. I was getting so confused by this concept of adding stuff to your plate when you already feel like it's all too much. But when I put it like this it makes sense. Sometimes the stuff that overwhelm us is actually stuff we signed up for ourselves but just didn't realize the effort it requires or something unexpected made us fall behind schedule. Adding stuff to that situation seems absolutely stupid D But if you think about the challenge as just taking an action, any action, toward something that makes you feel like you can make a difference then it makes sense. Here I am also reminded of a sentence from a previous video Take insufficient action. The stuff you're dealing with can be so big it can't be handled within one day. text:
Hello my beautiful fellow human beings. You don’t know me, and I don’t know you all, but allow me to introduce myself: I’ve been diagnosed with persistent depressive disorder in September 2019. It’s a form of chronic depression that I had to struggle with since I was 6-7 years old, but it went undiagnosed and untreated for many years, until I had a mental breakdown. 
I tried to kill myself two months after the diagnosis, when I finally realised that I might be condemned to feel that way for the rest of my life. 

Why am I telling you this ?

Because I can relate with the guilt you’re feeling right now. I too felt sorry for my loved ones, I felt guilty of being abnormal, guilty of not being happy, even though I seemingly had everything for me. I felt like my existence was an unfair burden that they had to unwillingly carry. 
It was terrible. I felt terrible. Like a monster in human form. 

But then, I received help. Firstly, from my therapists, who gave me an outlet to talk about my feelings, letting me understand what I was experiencing and why. Secondly, from my treatment, that nurtured my ill brain back to an chemical equilibrium, allowing me to see things a bit more clearly. 
And last but not least, from my loved ones. They reassured me of their love and care for me, made me understand that it wasn’t my fault if I was the way I was : I didn’t choose to be born this way, I didn’t choose to experience what I did, I didn’t choose to be depressed. I simply was. And because of that, I understood that the burden of my sickness, which was indeed real, was one they were more than willing to share with me.
Because they loved me. 
Even in the imperfection of my suffering, they loved me. 

So, if possible, don’t feel sorry for your loved ones, your parents, your family: more chance than none, they are more than willing to share the burden of our depression. Because they love us. And that’s what love is all about. 

Sharing is caring. 

I care about you all, 

Stay strong. Stay alive. It can get better, eventually

text:
I've done mechanical work on the various vehicles I've owned and it was all out of necessity. I remember I had this early 90s Volvo that kept ruining its alternator. My brother changed it for me a couple of times and I watched him do it but he wasn't able to do it one time and so my best friend and I decided that we would just try to do it. We had bought refurbished alternators several times at one of the auto parts places (don't remember which one now since it's been a couple of decades now) and so all we had to do was bring the busted one back and get another one. The thing about parts in some cars, and apparently Volvos are such cars, they don't have those parts in stock and so you have to wait until they ship one in. 

I've always had tools because I've fixed and built a lot of other things, so all I had to do was figure out how to get the alternator off the car and then how to put the new one on the car, but I had never done something that big on any of the cars I had owned up to that point since this was only my second car. So I had my best friend there with me to try to remember where all the different parts went so that we could put the new one on once we got it. Taking stuff apart is usually not terribly difficult but there's no point in taking it apart if you can't get it back together. So naturally, I just took out all the bolts holding the alternator and freed it from its belt. 

Then, since that was the only car we had and the alternator was a bit heavy for the several miles we had to walk to the auto parts place to give them that one and bring the new one back when it came in, we borrowed a shopping cart from the grocery store across the street both to take the broken alternator into the parts store and to bring the new one back. It always took them about a week to get another one for us so I had to remember how the alternator went in there for that entire time. At that point, we didn't have access to the internet at our apartment so I couldn't do what I would do now, which would be to look up how to do stuff online. I did at least have the maintenance manual for the car like I've had for every vehicle I have ever owned.

I was pretty nervous when I went to put the new alternator in but I managed to get it all together except for this long screw that went all the way through one side of the alternator. For whatever reason, it was kind of stuck when it was almost completely installed. I checked and rechecked and everything was lined up perfectly but I just couldn't screw it all the way in. Finally, I had strained so hard to get it to go that last little bit into place that I actually broke the screw in half! I was shocked and pretty stressed out because I didn't know what that screw was called so as to tell the parts store person what I needed. I also didn't have a camera to take a picture of any of this either to remember how things went together or to show anyone where I was having an issue. Luckily, the parts person was able to figure out which bolt I needed but I was really worried about it for a minute there because it seemed like an uncommonly long bolt. I've since broken several bolts on various vehicles, including a few bicycles, and it turns out that bolts aren't as strong as maybe they should be. When I broke that first bolt, I didn't know whether to stress out or to feel like I was uncommonly strong. lol

text:
I am a perfectionist, also probably got generalized anxiety as the cause of this, and I have been in pain for ages. I do have suicide attempts in my past (at the start of puberty, which will be interesting in a couple of paragraphs), but in my more recent life, everything is "great". I study just fine, completed my bachelors, went onto my masters programme, had a few friends, but mostly kept to myself. 

To be fair, I didnt quite realize how much pain I was in because I had supressed so much of it. For me, study, hobbies, and such became an escape, although always with the promise I made myself, that if I just achieved X, Y, Z, then I could feel happiness in this life. At that point in time, I did not realize, that noticing when you're happy with profound surprise "oh my, is this how happiness feels?!" probably means you should go see a therapist.

At some point, I even informed some friends of mine about the fact, that depressed people, if their mood suddenly gets vastly better, have decided to end it. They never realized that I was trying to reach out for help, nor did I really, although it felt incredibly important for me to make them aware about. 

My case might be a little niche, given that the reason I was supressing my own depression, promising myself that I would eventually be happy, and that surely it wasnt so bad right now, was gender incongruence (ICD-HA61) which is quite a mental mouthful to process in the first place. Regardless, I do relate a lot to Natalie, especially on the subject of shame. Interalized transphobia is really difficult to deal with, although it itself may be very niche (<1%) any stigma surrounding mental health may cause the same emotional patterns imo. 

I believe I am exiting a depression at the moment, which have lasted for so long, that I have forgotten when I stopped being able to feel joy or happiness (12+ years). Noone knew I was depressed, and my entire family was very surprised when I finally began talking about the things that are part of my life, and which will kill me unless I do something about it. In my case, I unfortunately cant resolve it just between myself, a therapist, and maybe some few close friends, I do need to involve every single person I've ever known to stop the sources of my suicidal throughts (getting misgendered, deadnamed, etc...) which is quite daunting, but so far I have been lucky outside of having to spend a lot of time teaching people about things they are blissfully unaware of. Its been quite the journey and it is nowhere near over (only been out for... 4-5 months now), but at least I finally, at the age of 25, fundementally want to exist, so thats nice.

text:
I feel like Karen takes some real scientific and psychological principles but she combines them with New Age psychobabble and well-placed buzz words and it really dilutes the message. DSM-V doesn't actually define trauma in the narrow ways that she describes; it doesn't only have to include explicitly violent or life-threatening situations. Neglect, negative social situations such as school bullying, or having a physically or mentally ill or incarcerated family member can all contribute to Adverse Childhood Experiences (as measured by the ACE Test). In addition, there have been many studies conducted on the long-term costs of childhood emotional abuse and neglect, which can sometimes lead to even longer-term mental health and self-esteem issues because children who are mercilessly criticized, ignored, or denied food, medical care, or affection often grow into adults with a deep sense of abandonment and the belief that their value as human beings is dependent on their performance or productivity. 

People with these kinds of problems are not just experiencing "burnout", they are very likely to have developed serious psychological problems such as depression, mood disorders, anxiety, addiction (including to caffeine like the man in the example given) that may require the treatment of mental health professionals and possibly a medical intervention. For many people whose illnesses have progressed to this point, hiring a life coach and just "getting in touch with your creativity and life's purpose" are not going to be enough; the work of dealing with early life trauma is extremely difficult and takes YEARS to complete. There are people who have been able to do the work without the help of medical professionals, but this requires a supportive system of family and/or friends, a healthy dose of introspection, and proper education on physical and mental health and wellness, as well as the willingness to utilize healthy coping skills (including but not limited to dietary adjustments and exercise). 

I also believe that we need to stop talking about cortisol and "the fight or flight response" in these dumbed-down, unscientific ways. Chronic stress truly does have extremely negative effects on your health, but cortisol is something that is required for human metabolism, it is the EXCESS production that causes the issues. You can reduce excess cortisol production by low-impact exercise or engaging in your hobbies in a meaningful way (like some of her clients did).  The YT Channel Therapy in a Nutshell explains what is really happening in the so-called "fight or flight response" when she describes the machinations of the sympathetic vs. the parasympathetic nervous system in the human body. 

Finally, the reason the definition of "burnout" has been limited to work-related fatigue by the WHO organization is due to the fact that, as I expressed, there are other mental health terms that can better explain what is happening with some of Karen's clients. Karen, from what I can tell, is not a psychologist, so I do not believe she has a right to arbitrarily redefine a term that has been created SPECIFICALLY to explain work-related fatigue and dissatisfaction and disillusionment related to job satisfaction. The reason why burnout didn't encompass what was happening to Karen's clients is because they weren't experiencing burnout! Also, to assume that workplace dissatisfaction doesn't interact with "systemic racism" is absurd and really shows that authors like Karen have no understanding of how chronic stress at a job that requires long hours and does not provide financial stability can take a psychological toll on minority workers that WILL bleed into the rest of our lives; in fact, ANY GROUP,  including poor white people, locked into physically demanding, unrewarding jobs is bound to incur physical and psychological strain that could affect them long-term and will negatively affect other areas of their lives. 

It's really that simple.

I know life can be f*cking hard. I’ve been depressed and had suicidal thoughts. Sometimes you cannot find a reason to keep on going! BUT! even living for someone else is a reason. I’m still here because of my parents and boyfriend, they were my reason to keep going. Now 5 years later, yes I still have down moments, but I found the love within me again, I enjoy going out again, I love giving love to others! 

If anyone reads this and wants to have some coping mechanisms, 1 get structure back in your life. Sleep and wake up at the same times every day. Doesn’t matter if you cannot get anything done that day. Just keep doing it until it gets easier and easier. 2 believe the people around you. You are loved and you will be missed. Do it for them, then slowly the fight will be for yourself. 3 talk about it. It can be really uplifting to tell your feelings. Don’t be embarrassed or feel guilty, depression can happen to everyone no matters the circumstances. Tell a psychiatrist, friend or family, it doesn’t matter, but sometimes hearing yourself can have a great effect.

Please keep going, every person on this planet deserves a place, deserves love and deserves to find happiness

text:
I get a type of anxiety attack I don’t hear people talking about. I think it’s because I have Bipolar II with Rapid Cycling Severe Anxious Distress. Basically I call it “The Pit” bc it’s as close to Hell as you can experience without being in literal Hell. It’s a horrible mix of Cognitive Constriction, so I can’t think outside what I’m immediately experiencing; which is a Severe Anxiety Attack, with a Mixed Episode of Dysphoric Hypomania, Crippling Suicidal Depression, and Disassociation all at once. It lasts anywhere from 30mins to 6 hours.

STAGE 1: It usually starts off with the immediate feeling of “oh shit, it’s gunna get dark.” I start having ruminating and racing thoughts about everything that’s troubling me. It can be little things or it can be my past trauma. I start to get the beginning symptom of anxiety. My heart will beat faster, my thoughts will get faster, my breathing will get faster, and the creeping in of the doom feelings start.
STAGE 2: This causes me to slip into or more rapidly into a Severe Depressive Ep. I get a feeling of agonizing depression in a void or bubble, separate from everyone and everything.The utter aloneness and helplessness creeps in, and the negative self talk, hopelessness, helplessness, etc kick in and repeat bc of the racing thoughts. It’s like a cloud of all the bad things surrounds me, and my vision gets wonky. It becomes darker and I get tunnel vision.
STAGE 3: Then the anxiety attack comes into full play. The hyperventilating is making me dizzy, I can’t stop crying, or shaking, and then I get the need to run away, but I can’t because I feel like I’m in my own bubble of horror. I want to stop this all so bad I begin to dissociate. I can’t think straight at all, and coping skills DO NOT work and I don’t know why. 
STAGE 4: All this all gets kicked into higher gear because of the Depressive Ep turning into a Severe Mixed Episode due to the start of the Hypomanic Ep or it starting faster because of the way I feel the need to run or do something, anything, to stop it all. Basically the Flight, Fight, and Shutdown System triggers my Hypomania, which I guess would be good if I was chased by some Mountain Lion. Hypomania for me is almost always dysphoric which make some feel like my body is burning because it’s so uncomfortable and foreign, my clothes feel so wrong as well. Eventually, due to the 4X increase in the intensity of all the symptoms, all I feel is my mind and body.
STAGE 5: Dysphoria causes the trapped in a bubble, can’t feel outside what I’m experiencing, and fog of horrible ruminating fast thoughts to make me dissociate like I’m out of my body but also fully aware and feeling. The rational and in control part of me is what dissociates which I guess could be why I can’t use coping skills with these ones. I literally stop knowing where I am because it gets so dark, and all my senses are occupied with flash backs to traumatic things to register where I am.
STAGE 6: The only thing I think of to make it stop (especially when it’s hours on end,) is self harm and suicide as my only way out. Self-harm has helped to stop it but I’m so addicted it’s to the point where I cut deep enough for 22 really complex surgical stitches. I fight these thoughts til I’m on the brink. So I sit, lay or stay in whatever position I’m in for hours to deal with the shit storm of all the bad symptoms of my mental illnesses occurring at once.

The only thing... person, who has been able to stop these attacks is my Pastor. Not necessarily for religious reasons, but because he’s the only person I trust with everything, and has been there for me unlike everyone else.

You may have suicidal thoughts when you come off the medication that isn't uncommon just ride through it and one of two things will happen the chemicals in your head could level out for a long time or you may need to stay on medication or do what I do and listen to self guided meditation on youtube try micheal sealey anxiety talkdown trust me it will help you sleep and save you a world of pain. Oleh karena itu banyak orang yang tidak tahu penyakil mental ini dan tidak memperdulikannya, padahal sangat penting untuk dijaga. Berikut ada beberapa hal yang perlu dilakukan untuk lower this mental health yaitu pertama rasakan anda mengatur hidup anda, jadi kayak you control of your life. Karena jika mengatur hidup sendiri merasa baik dalam segi mental, seperti memilih baju, makanan, pekerjaan dll.  Ada quote dari Poet GK Chesterton yaitu “anything worth doing is worth doing badly the first time” jadi artinya adalah sesuatu yang bagus dikerjakan adalah saat pekerjaan itu dilakukan dengan buruk untuk pertama kalinya. Jadi wajar dan malah bagus kalau kita mau melakukan sesuatu pertama kali walaupun hasilnya salah. Karena masih banyak orang malah belum memulainya daripada doing badly. Dan untuk second coping strategy adalah is to forgive yourself. Jadi artinya banyak orang anxiety takut akan pendapat orang lain, reaksi orang lain, apapun pendapat orang lain terhadap dirinya, takut berbuat salah apalagi di hidupnya. text: Feeling overwhelmed can be successfully dealt with by understanding the relationship between passive and active challenges. Passive challenges are difficulties imposed on us, while active challenges are ones we choose to take on. Feeling overwhelmed occurs when passive challenges outweigh active challenges. Increasing the number of active challenges can help combat overwhelm. The principle of increasing active challenges applies not only to eating disorders but also to treatments for depression. Behavioral activation, taking on small challenges, can help gain control of life and alleviate depression. Taking control of unrelated challenges can help change our mindset and feel confident in tackling overwhelming problems. Unplugging or disarming the feeling of overwhelm is achieved by increasing active challenges and shifting the cognitive equation.

For years I thought it was a point of pride to be the person that was told, “I don’t know how you do it” on a regular basis. It became my gauge to know when I might be slacking.
This is not a good long term plan and I had what I consider a “mental breakdown”. 
I was caring for my mother who was losing her battle with cancer. I was caring for my teenager with nonverbal autism and seizures. At the same time I was being triangulated and in a terrible relationship. 
One day I tried to get medication my son needed and couldn’t. 
It was the straw… it was like my ability to hold any more fear worry loss or emotional pain was at capacity. I lost my ability to speak and couldn’t drive anywhere. It was like the world was a different place and I no longer knew how to navigate in it. I tried to call family and was able to say where I was, my son is sitting in the back of my car this whole time. My sister showed up to take me to the hospital and as soon as she asked me a question this sound came out of me I had never heard from anyone. I have only realized today what the sound was and it has been 6 years. It was keening. In the hospital someone asked a question and I started keening again. 
I was given an injection of Ativan and it all stopped and I was able to speak and everything else. I went to a doctor and was told that wasn’t a mental breakdown. At the same time she told me I was close to losing myself. I’m not sure of the difference.

text:
In my opinion, the primary cause of depression is having no Loving purpose in life, no reason to be alive, no Joy to be had from even existing, because there’s no end to your pain. It most often manifests after certain events that make you feel as if there’s just no point doing anything anymore. Such as the loss of loved ones, relationship breakdown, family breakup, loss of income, retirement and old age, physical or mental harm, until life itself becomes depressing. 

From my own personal experience, depression can be more easily solved by finding a selfless Spiritual Goal that allows you to let go of your pain. Whilst gradually winding down the so called “medication” that will actually hinder your mental capacity to achieve that end. If you belong to any Spiritual Pathway you always have the goal of doing good deeds to build heaven on earth and enjoy heaven in subsequent lives, which should save you from depressive states of mind. 

But most importantly, if you are suffering during very difficult times, having Faith in something or someone that you know is good and can lead to your salvation from pain and suffering, can help you get through those difficulties. Without Faith, you may search and find nothing at all worth living for, so you feel there is no hope for you. This is why you should find Learned Spiritual Teachers, learn their Spiritual Principles, focus on understanding them in depth, and Practice in line with that. 

It’s important to note that even the most seemingly mundane day to day activity can be transformed through Wisdom into a more meaningful Spiritual Endeavour. If the underlying activity is able to be selflessly purified in terms of some lasting benefit to yourself and others instead of just the temporary stimulation of your senses. The failure to do so is why depression is more prevalent in societies driven by short-term sensual greed rather than long-term spirituality.

For those who are dealing with clinically depressed loved ones, it is critically important to not attribute blame on them for their problem. Also to not get angry or upset if they are unwilling to do the same things they could easily do before. But to seek out their help and encourage whatever assistance they can give you instead of viewing that as being just annoying or pointless. Because your goal should be to help them slowly find some purpose and some reason for living. 

Bearing in mind there are no chemical solutions to depression because it is entirely the domain of the conceptual mind.

text:
That is so interesting on so many levels, how different his experience is to mine. For me it was the easiest thing to share my struggles with my friend my psychologist and really anyone that I remotely connected with, even if they were just encounters of one night on a random festival or in a bar. Talking about my depression has never been hard for me, but it also did not get me a single step closer to healing. 
I did a very similar thing to him. I walked the Camino de Santiago in Spain. 1000km in 5 weeks with a friend of mine and I met tons of interessting people and I did enjoy life during that time. Some of my encounters introduced me to "workaway" which is working for nothing but accomodation and food for private households. Helping them with anything imaginable, from building fences, over hearding llamas, to watching children, helping with the harvest, driving bulldozers and cuting trees or even helping to birth a calf. I did so many things over the course of 2 years. But it came to an end, because I still had to pay insurance and I had no income at all, i lived off my savings. There was no room for me to earn money, so my adventure of healing came to an end. And it didn't take a week for my depression to come back and it is worse than it ever was, because I know what I want to do, but society does not allow me to do it. There is no way for me to do what I love for an indefinate amount of time and that is frustrating. UBI would be a way to help me, but that is probably decades off.

I have been living with depression for about 15 years now, which is exactly half of my life and I don't see a way out of it. Not by talking and not by doing what he is doing, because it is not sustainable in the long run. 
I have a very similar view as him about suicide. Like it being not an option at all, it is the worst thing you can do to leave people behind hurt, wondering if they could have done something or should have done more.
What I want from my life is a legal way to say goodbye to my loved ones, explain to them that I do not want to be anymore, and leave on good terms with them with the aid of a proffesional. Similar to how we release our pets from their pain towards the end of their lives and they can't even express their wishes. Humans can and still we are forced to live or die by our own hand in a horrible way for everyone involved.

So yes, I can answer the question: I really want to die. Because not feeling the way I am feeling is always temporary and the depression is creeping back the first chance it gets and I don't want to live a life in fear of not being able to stay ahead of it.

text:
- analyze your anxiety 
Ask yourself what thought made you feel that way, or what happened to make you feel that way.
- once you find the source of your problem.. (everybody has different triggers) you need to go pursue whatever it is that you are afraid of. 
Ex. I use to have anxiety so bad I was scared to drive my car.. because I thought something was gonna happen to me… the more you isolate yourself form your fears the worse your anxiety is gonna get. One day i told myself I’m gonna go drive my car.. I was so afraid, but I pushed forward, and drove my car.. I realized that I was actually ok. 
You have to not allow fear to isolate you. 

At first I didn’t know, but what triggered my anxiety was my )acid reflux) it would happen , and it would feel like I couldn’t breath .. then I would feel like I was gonna die then I would (hyperventilate ) which causes your body to release adrenaline which makes your heart rate go up, and breathing rate! If you continue to hyperventilate you’ll end having an anxiety attack!

(NOTICE)when your breathing at a fast rate then slow down your breathing.

So I started to take my acid reflux medicine , and I started to conquer my fears ! , and it went away!

If fear is the reason you isolate then that’s a problem! 

If you isolate to focus that’s fine , but don’t isolate for too long.. it’s gonna put you in your mind .. you need to be able to get all those thoughts out of your mind (talk to people). We all need each other honestly . 

When your having a panic attack the reason why areas of your body goes numb is because of rapid breathing.. 
this causes your body to decrease carbon dioxide in the blood your blood vessels begin to constrict, and your body shuts off blood flow to less essential areas of your body. in order to keep blood flowing where you need it most. As blood flows away from your fingers, toes, and face, these areas may feel numb or tingly.

I did the research for you, but in order to over come we must understand.

I hope this helps! If it does give Jesus the glory not me .. he showed me the way when I was going through it

text:
EMDR and somatic experiencing helped me tremendously on the unconscious level.

CBT was interesting on the conscious level, helping me to create distance from my thoughts and not give them any importance. Because we don’t control the arrival of thoughts and sensations — the only power we have is in how we respond to them.

The great key is acceptance of everything that can happen to you. If you can accept the possibility of losing everything, going insane, being alone, or even dying, then your anxiety will melt away like snow in the sun. But at first, your ego will make you tremble with fear because it wants to protect you from repressed emotions. Become an observer of your reactions, your emotions, your thoughts.

Your body is intelligent; its one and only goal is to protect you and help you survive. But your ego is so afraid of emotions, thoughts, and death that it blocks the potential healing that your body and mind are trying to bring about. Give it space, and you’ll see that it knows what to do. It knows what it's time to heal, and anxiety — like intrusive thoughts — is simply the result of an ego that is blocking that healing. Surrender the fight.
